http://i.imgur.com/rNGifjV.jpg

This is a gun I've always wanted, but I never wanted it quite enough to pay full price. It's spent years - decades, honestly - on that list in the back of my mind, one of those guns to snap up when a good deal comes into view.

A few weeks back, Sportsman's Outdoors had a pile of them, used, police-trade guns, for $377 shipped. They were sold out within a couple of hours, but I got lucky this time and snagged one.

Internet rumor suggests these came from the Texas Department of Public Safety Narcotics Unit. P232SLs are not a commonly issued gun.

Mine arrived like most police trade-ins I've purchased, filthy and scuffed, but mechanically in fine shape. I field stripped it, removed the new-looking plastic grips, and hosed it down with aerosol break cleaner. After letting it dry in the sun I hosed it down again with aerosol Rem Oil, lightly greased the rails and the spring tunnel, installed a new $7 recoil spring and called it good. Once clean she was much improved, acting and feeling much more like a nicely machined pistol instead of a sticky, gummy train wreck. The scuffs are still there but none of them are very deep, and they could be polished out if I ever cared to do so. The old recoil spring was just as long as the new one I replaced it with, and there was only modest evidence of wear inside, just a few small shiny spots worn through the matt stainless finish. She'd been shot some, but not very much. The KK date code tells me she was made in 1999.

Before I offer my opinion on this gun, I'd like to digress for a minor but relevant rant. I think it's silly to treat every center-fire handgun as if it were a serious fighting gun, and to evaluate it solely on that basis. I do have a pistol or two that are dedicated for defensive use, and the rest are there for fun. Call them collectibles or range toys or whatever you like, I own them and shoot them because they make me happy. Guys who collect motorcycles seem to understand that most of the time, it's all about enjoyment and style and history rather than sheer performance, but too many gun guys seem to be forgetting this lately.

That said, I do not consider the P232 to be an adequate defensive gun. It's just too big and heavy for a 7+1 .380. Here is in in comparison to the 6+1 Colt Mustang and the Kel-Tec P3AT:

http://i.imgur.com/Np12EeW.jpg

It also kicks too hard and is too difficult to rack, the DA/SA trigger and heel magazine release are outdated, and it is overly complex and too expensive, and on top of all that, it's been discontinued by the maker, making parts and service harder to find. I'm pretty sure there are 9mms that are not any bigger or heavier, or any harder to shoot well. Defensive use is serious stuff, and there's really only two choices - there's the gun that best fits your needs, and there's the guns that are inadequate substitutes. There's nothing in between.

Of course I couldn't care less about any of that. Zombie killing aside, my impression is that this is a very nice little pistol, and that's what I got it for. The DA trigger is smooth and easy to manage, the SA trigger is spot-on, and the sights, especially for a gun of this size, are quite good, with bright orange plastic dots installed front and rear and lots of daylight in between. It fits my hand very well and the trigger reach and the balance is just right.

http://i.imgur.com/BA1kq1y.png

I very much enjoy the build quality of this gun. The slide, which is surprising hard to rack if you don't cock the hammer first, is closely fitted to the frame without a hint of gap or wiggle. The slide serrations stick right into your fingers when you grip them, not uncomfortably, but very securely. There's a perfectly-executed spot of red paint on a machined recess of the extractor, acting as an inoffensive loaded-chamber indicator. The take-down lever and hammer drop lever are positive and secure and move like they are on rails. Except for the slide serrations, there are no sharp edges anywhere. If there are any machine marks to seen I haven't found them yet.

http://i.imgur.com/Y7jhmxf.jpg

I've only run about 50 round through it so far, cheap aluminum-cased Blazer hardball, which worked without a hitch. My steel targets rang with an unaccustomed regularity, which was nice. Recoil was a bit sharper than I expected, even with a new spring, but there was no slide bite or trigger slap. It felt like shooting a really nice compact 9mm.

This is one of those pistols which is greater than the sum of its parts. It fits, it works, everything is nice, and it always seems to hit whatever you point it at. When you put it down you sort of want to pick it up again.

I have a couple of similar guns - an East German Makarov and a CZ-82, and a VZ-50 and Walther PP, both in .32acp. I'd say the CZ-82 is the most utilitarian of the bunch, but it requires that the hammer be manually lowered over a live round if the gun is to be carried, unless you want to trust the thumb safety alone and carry it in condition one. The Walther has tiny sights and will bite my hand if I'm not careful. The VZ-50 has a surprisingly modern, three position safety/decock that also allows for condition one carry, unlike the two-position safety/decock of the Walther and the Mak, where the safety can only be applied if the hammer is already down. Of the five, the 232 has by far the best trigger and the best sights.

http://i.imgur.com/YzbhcMk.jpg

The only thing I don't like about it is that when it is field stripped and the slide removed, there is a large flat part - the slide lock, I think - which is not securely attached to the side of the frame. It's held on only with a spring, and when you put your hand against it, it shifts out of place, making you worry that that you are about to twist the spring out of shape or drop the parts on the ground.

http://i.imgur.com/MFNGqKn.jpg http://i.imgur.com/p0Gics1.jpg

It's a minor quibble, but that's all I've got.

If you're talking ultralight, GORP and gatorade packets. If you're talking mostly light, any of the freeze dried offerings from White Mountain are pretty decent. Is this automobile camping or hiking camping. Where as automobile camping is where you set up next to your car or RV and hiking camping is well hiking somewhere and camping. The latter of the two needs to focus more on lighter foods.

I am going to talk mostly about car camping.

  1. I like to pre-scramble my eggs at home and put them in a Blender bottle. They take up less space in the cooler and portion control is much easier.

  2. You can take small snack size ziploc bags, chop up all your veggies (bell peppers, onions, tomato, ham, etc) and put them and the scrambled egg premix into the ziploc. Make sure to get as much air out as possible, seal it up, and boil it in water for 10-15 min. let cool they are like pretty cool. Also most recipes I find online say 13 min eggs-actly.

  3. Add marinade to your meat and freeze it the night before you leave. It will act as an ice block in the cooler, just remember to take it out a hour or two before you cook it. And when the marinade freezes it will form crystals that will allow the marinade to penetrate deeper when it is thawed.

  4. Don't forget "Pogey bait" lol. Well that what I call it anyhow. Its just a really candy trailmix. you can add healthy stuff if you want... But i usually add a bunch of m&m's, Reese's pieces, peanuts, cashews, and anything else that sounds good. great to put in a container and pass it around the camp fire.
